extracted.intended_audience: linguists, humor researchers, and students studying semantics and joke theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Raskin's Script-Based Semantic Theory of Humor to analyze whether a single-joke text is humorous by checking script compatibility, opposition, triggers, and audience knowledge. Useful for linguistic analysis and formal explanation of joke mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 1: Script Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The text must be fully or in part compatible with two different scripts. Most of the text is ambiguous — it can be interpreted under either script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility must be genuine semantic overlap, not a forced reinterpretation. Examples of scripts: DOCTOR (medical office, white coat, examination...), MARRIAGE (ceremony, vows, rings...), DEATH (corpse, funeral...). When analyzing, ask: what two scripts does the text invoke? Is the text genuinely compatible with both?

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 2: Script Opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The two scripts evoked must be opposite in a specific technical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Raskin provides a hierarchy of oppositions to identify this technical 'opposite':
- Most abstract: REAL vs. UNREAL.
- Mid-level: ACTUAL vs. NON-ACTUAL; NORMAL vs. ABNORMAL; POSSIBLE vs. IMPOSSIBLE.
- Most concrete (basic oppositions): GOOD vs. BAD; LIFE vs. DEATH; OBSCENE vs. NON-OBSCENE; MONEY vs. NO MONEY; HIGH STATUS vs. LOW STATUS.
These opposition axes are what make the switch from one script to another produce humorous force; the five basic oppositions are argued to capture the vast majority of jokes. When analyzing, identify the opposition axis that distinguishes Script A from Script B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger that licenses the script switch
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a trigger (often the punchline) that reveals that Script B has also been compatible all along and licenses the switch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trigger is usually localized (commonly the punchline) and it forces the audience to reinterpret earlier material under the alternative script. When evaluating, locate the specific element that forces the script switch: what word/phrase/event reveals Script B?

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience possession of both scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must possess both scripts. A joke fails when the listener doesn't know one of the scripts being invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators must consider the audience's cultural/experiential knowledge; if the audience lacks one script, the required interpretation and thus the humor will not occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine opposition, not mere difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The two scripts must contradict on one of the recognized opposition axes; mere unrelatedness or mere difference is not sufficient for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If scripts are only different but not opposed (i.e., they do not lie on an opposition axis like good/bad or real/unreal), the result may be clever but not funny. Ask: is there a contradiction along an opposition axis?

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary process/unfolding of the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical unfolding: (1) The text is consistent with Script A from the beginning; (2) a trigger reveals that Script B has also been compatible all along; (3) the audience switches from A to B (or holds both simultaneously); (4) the opposition between A and B is what gives the switch its humorous force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence as a procedural diagnostic when determining whether a text functions as a single-joke-carrying text according to SSTH. Consider whether the audience is likely to perform the switch or to hold both scripts simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: single-script compatibility (no joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts compatible with only one script are excluded — they do not constitute jokes under SSTH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analysis shows only one viable script interpretation throughout the text, classify it as non-jocular according to SSTH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: two scripts without opposition (clever but not funny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts compatible with two scripts that are merely different but not opposed are excluded — they may be clever but are not funny according to SSTH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the two scripts are opposed on one of the recognized axes; if not, SSTH predicts lack of humor despite script multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: two scripts without a trigger (no licensed switch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts requiring two scripts but lacking a trigger to license the switch are excluded — without a trigger the audience is not led to the intended reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for a localized element that forces reinterpretation; absent such a trigger, the presence of two scripts does not produce humor per SSTH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for SSTH analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of questions to diagnose whether a text meets SSTH's conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specific diagnostic questions: What two scripts does the text invoke? Is the text genuinely compatible with both? What is the opposition axis (real/unreal, good/bad, sex/non-sex, etc.)? Where is the trigger — what specific element forces the script switch? Does the audience plausibly know both scripts?
